why: Replays the NO-1/§6.2 void rule. The rule moved from the weak trace form `{any_of:[{tool:'*',denied:true}]}` — which voided on ANY denial of ANY tool, including one the scenario declared and one the product's governor decided deliberately — to the strong `denial` detector reading `undeclared`, which subtracts declared denials, role-disallowed tools, and governor-decided ones. These cases therefore supply `denials` + `intended_denials` rather than a trace carrying `denied` flags, because the new rule reads the denial record, not the per-call flag. Amended: the first positive case was named 'a governor denial on Bash' and asserted the detector FIRES — asserting that a governor decision counts as undeclared, which is the opposite of what this rule exists to do and of what this file's own `why` says. It pinned the pre-fix behaviour in the case named after the fix. Renamed to what it actually tests, and the two advertised subtractions that no case exercised — governor-decided denials, and tools the bench never granted — now have one positive and one negative each.

positive.name: a denial with no governor log entry — the bench's own allowlist
a denied spawn the scenario never declared
an undeclared denial among successful calls
a governor entry for a DIFFERENT target does not excuse this denial

negative.name: a tool that returned an error is not a denial
a denial the scenario DECLARED is not undeclared
a denial of a tool the ROLE disallows is the role's own boundary
a denial the product's GOVERNOR decided, matched on (tool,target)
a tool the bench never granted is a declared constraint, not an incidental denial
